layers.note: A canopy tree of floodplains, stream banks and lake shores.

moisture.note: Wet ground near water: floodplains, gravel bars and shores.

elevation_m.note: Sea level to about 900 m in western Washington; the upper limits are loose.

max_slope_deg.note: On flats and gentle slopes along water.

coldest_c.note: Maritime and inland winters both: coldest-month means from about −10 °C (gone by −16 °C), as from the coast to the interior mountains.

hard_freeze_c.note: Cold-hardy: lows to about −34 °C borne, gone where the year's coldest night falls below about −42 °C.

warmest_c.note: Across its range, warmest-month means from about 11.5 to 25 °C; gone below 9 °C, where summers are too short, and above 28.5 °C.

degree_days_0.note: About 1,800 or more degree-days above 0 °C, none below 1,100.

degree_days_5.note: About 800 or more degree-days above 5 °C, none below 400: from the lowlands to the montane forest.

moisture_index.note: It grows where the ground stays wet whatever the climate's moisture index, so only the driest climates (below about 0.1) rule it out; the site's own moisture places it.

summer_rain.note: No lower limit; its range takes in summer-dry coasts and interior mountains with some summer rain, to about 0.45 of the year's precipitation.

provenance.notes: Authored from general knowledge of the species in the south Puget Sound lowlands; not yet checked against the public-domain USDA references (Silvics of North America, the Fire Effects Information System, PLANTS). Climate ranges (niche schema 2, 2026-10-06): Black cottonwood grows on bottomlands from Alaska to Baja California's mountains and east to the Rockies (Silvics of North America, vol. 2). Each climate range brackets the climate of that range at the 2.8° ERA5 product's scale, an approximate envelope read from these descriptions, not fitted to occurrence records.
